title: Modules, packages and the standard library

videos.script:
The most useful habit in this course is one line long: before you write it, look for it. {{look}} Somebody has already written it, they have tested it on more machines than you will ever see, and on your computer it is already installed.

{{std}} That is the standard library, and it is the reason Python is worth knowing as well as the language. Dates, paths, counting things, reading JSON, random numbers, regular expressions, command-line arguments — all of it is one `import` away, with no dependency to add and nothing to install.

{{cost}} The cost of not knowing it is not that you cannot do the thing. It is that you write forty lines that mostly work: a date parser that is wrong in February, a path join that breaks on the machine that uses a different separator, a counter that is a dictionary and six lines of `if key in`.

{{module}} A module is a file. That is the whole concept — `math.py` somewhere on this machine, and `import math` makes its names available. A package is a directory of those. Everything about imports follows from that.

{{path}} And the half that goes wrong is where Python LOOKS. It searches a list, and the first entry is the directory you are in — so a file you called `random.py` is found before the library, and the error you get names a function that exists, in a file you wrote, saying something is missing. It is a ten-minute confusion the first time and thirty seconds every time after, once you know to look.

{{tour}} The middle of this lesson is a tour: ten modules, one line each on what they are FOR. You are not expected to remember the functions. You are expected to remember that the thing exists, so that the next time you need it, you look instead of writing it.

{{four}} Then four of them properly — `pathlib`, `datetime`, `collections` and `itertools` — because those four change how the rest of this course is written.

One question, answered three ways. The question: what does `str.partition` do when the separator is not there?

{{docs}} First, the documentation. `docs.python.org`, search for `str.partition`, and it is a paragraph: it returns a three-tuple, and if the separator is not found, the first element is the whole string and the other two are empty. That is the authoritative answer and it took fifteen seconds.

{{help}} Second, without a browser. In the interpreter, `help(str.partition)`. The same sentence, from the docstring, on the machine I am already typing on — and it works on a server with no network, which is where I usually need it.

{{source}} Third, the source. `import inspect` and `inspect.getsource` for anything written in Python — `pathlib`, `json`, `collections`. `str` is written in C so this one has no source to show, and that refusal is itself information: the answer for a built-in type is the documentation.

{{which}} Which to use: `help()` when you have forgotten the arguments, the docs when you want the edge cases, and the source when the documentation says something surprising and you want to see why.

{{tab}} And the fourth thing, which is not a question at all: `dir(module)` lists what is in it, and pressing Tab in the interpreter does the same thing interactively. That is how you find out that `itertools` has something for your problem without reading the whole page.

Import it before you write it, and know where Python looked.

{{library}} Ten modules were named in this lesson and you are not meant to have memorised them. What is worth carrying is the shape of the question: a date, a path, counting, a file format, a random choice, a pattern — one of those is in the standard library, and looking takes less time than the first attempt at writing it.

{{four}} Four of them are worth being fluent in. `pathlib`, because a path is an object and not a string. `datetime`, because the naive one has no time zone and that is the bug everybody ships once. `collections`, for `Counter` and `defaultdict`, which between them delete a great deal of code. And `itertools`, for the four that earn their import.

{{imports}} `import module` and then `module.thing` is the default, because a reader can see where the name came from. `from module import thing` when the name is used constantly. And never `import *`, which puts names in your file that nothing in your file mentions.

{{path}} And the shadowing. If an import fails in a way that makes no sense, look for a file of yours with that name in the directory you are in. Python looked there first, and it found you.
